headline: Gut's Hidden Repair System: How Berries and Pomegranates Fight IBD
meta_description: Researchers discover how urolithin A, a compound from pomegranates and berries, activates a protective pathway that repairs the gut lining in IBD patients.
summary_short: University of Louisville researchers found that a metabolite from pomegranates and berries can trigger gut cells to repair themselves rather than inflame—offering hope f…
body:
Researchers at the University of Louisville have mapped a precise mechanism by which compounds in pomegranates, walnuts, and berries could help repair damaged intestinal tissue in inflammatory bowel disease patients. When gut bacteria break down these foods, they produce a metabolite called urolithin A. The team, led by associate professor Venkatakrishna Rao Jala, discovered that urolithin A activates a protein called the aryl hydrocarbon receptor specifically in intestinal epithelial cells—the cells forming the gut lining itself. This targeted activation triggers a protective cellular response that repairs tissue, strengthens the intestinal barrier, boosts mucus production, and defends against harmful microbes. The findings, published in Nature Communications, represent the first detailed tracing of this mechanism in human tissue, moving the research from theory into clinical relevance.

What makes this discovery striking is the contrast it reveals. The same receptor that toxins can activate—causing inflammation—can be switched toward healing when activated by the right dietary compound in the right location. Most existing IBD treatments work broadly, suppressing the immune system across the body. This pathway offers something different: a targeted repair mechanism that addresses the root problem. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis affect millions globally, and both involve a deteriorating intestinal barrier that becomes a feedback loop of worsening inflammation.

While no clinical therapy yet exists, Jala's team has spent years studying urolithin A's effects. Researcher Sweta Ghosh emphasized that the findings challenge assumptions: some inflammatory pathways, when properly activated in the right cells, support healing rather than harm. Whether urolithin A becomes a viable drug or serves primarily as a key to understanding how to unlock this protective pathway, the mechanism is now mapped and tested in human tissue—a significant step toward more precise, restoration-focused treatments.
quick_facts: University of Louisville researchers led by Venkatakrishna Rao Jala
Urolithin A from pomegranates, walnuts, and berries activates gut repair
Findings tested in cell models, organoids, and tissue from IBD patients
Compound targets intestinal lining cells, not immune cells broadly
